analysis.one_liner: Ends federally subsidized bank student loans and puts the savings into Pell Grants, community colleges, and early learning programs.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 253–171 with 247 of 253 Democrats voting yes, but died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have shut down the program under which private banks issued student loans backed by a federal guarantee, ending June 2010, and put the savings into Pell Grants for low-income students, community college and construction programs, and a new early learning fund for low-income children. It also simplified how families qualify for aid, offered loan relief to service members called to duty, and hired support officers for veterans on campus. The House passed it, but the Senate never acted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income students and their families: the bill guaranteed full funding of the maximum Pell Grant and automatic increases tied to inflation plus 1% [S4]. It simplified the aid application by excluding pension assets and most untaxed income from the family-need calculation and preserved aid eligibility for students convicted of simple drug possession [S4]. Veterans got campus resource officers, loan forgiveness when called to duty, and children of fallen public safety officers got automatic maximum Pell eligibility [S4]. Low-income children under five would have gained a new Early Learning Challenge Fund, and community college students would have benefited from construction grants and reform grants under the American Graduation Initiative [S4]. School construction grants required prevailing wages for laborers and American-made iron and steel [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income students and community college students

how_it_helps.text: Fully funds the maximum Pell Grant and raises it by $490 for 2008-09 and 2009-10 and $690 for 2010-11, with automatic increases thereafter tied to the Consumer Price Index plus 1%
Prohibits any new loans under the bank-based Federal Family Education Loan program after June 30, 2010, ending federal subsidies and guarantees to private student lenders

Creates a $600 million-per-year College Access and Completion Innovation Fund and grants for community college construction and reform, with priority for low-income, first-generation, and veteran students
Establishes the Early Learning Challenge Fund to expand high-quality early learning programs for disadvantaged children under five

Simplifies aid eligibility by excluding pension plans, child support, and veterans' benefits from the family need calculation, and preserves eligibility for students convicted of drug possession rather than sale

Waits out loan repayment and forgives loans for students called to military service, funds Veterans Resource Officers on campuses, and sets the expected family contribution to zero for children of fallen public safety officers
Directs grants for modernizing public school and community college facilities, requiring prevailing wages for construction laborers and mechanics

analysis.who_pays: Private banks and lenders lost the federally guaranteed student loan business the bill would have ended. Families with more than $150,000 in net assets would have become ineligible for Pell Grants and Direct Loans [S4]. States and colleges had to put up matching funds for the innovation, community college, and Perkins loan programs [S4]. Students taking out Direct Loans after June 2012 would face variable interest rates, capped at 6.8% [S4]. The bill also gave for-profit colleges a third consecutive year to fail the rule requiring 10% of revenue from non-federal-aid sources before losing aid eligibility, easing a protection for students [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student lenders and wealthier families

drawbacks.text: Students whose families have more than $150,000 in combined net assets (inflation-adjusted) become ineligible for Pell Grants and Direct Loans, regardless of other circumstances
Undergraduate Direct Loans made after June 2012 carry variable interest rates set off Treasury bill rates rather than fixed rates, capped at 6.8%

The bill loosens the 90/10 rule protecting students from schools dependent on federal aid: for-profit colleges get three consecutive years (up from two) of failing the rule before losing federal aid eligibility, and revenue from the 2008 unsubsidized loan limit increase continues to count as non-federal revenue
The Defund ACORN Act bars federal funds to any organization whose employees or affiliates have been indicted, not convicted, for election-law violations, denying funding on accusation alone
State innovation, community college, and Perkins loan programs require matching funds from states and colleges, limiting participation by the poorest institutions

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is strong for ordinary people: ending lender subsidies frees money for Pell Grant increases, community colleges, and early learning, and the aid simplification removes real paperwork and penalty problems. The asset cap is a genuine cut that could exclude some middle-class families with high home or savings equity but low cash flow, and variable rates after 2012 introduce uncertainty even with the 6.8% ceiling. The for-profit college concession weakens a consumer protection, and the ACORN provision sets a precedent of denying funds on indictment rather than conviction. On balance the benefits to low-income students and families outweigh these costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but after the Senate received the bill it sat in the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 15, 2009 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which ordered it reported by a 30–17 vote and reported it amended on July 27
The House adopted the Republican motion to recommit adding the Defund ACORN Act by a 345–75 vote (Roll no. 718), with 172 Democrats and all 173 voting Republicans in favor
The House passed the bill on September 17, 2009, 253–171 (Roll no. 719): 247 of 253 House Democrats voted yes and only 4 no, while just 6 of 178 House Republicans voted yes and 167 voted no

The Senate received the bill on September 21, 2009 and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the next day; the record shows no further action for the rest of the 111th Congress
The bill never received a Senate committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private lenders and loan middlemen whose federally guaranteed student loan business the bill would have ended kept that business instead; low-income students and families did not receive the promised Pell Grant increases, early learning fund, or community college investments through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private student lenders and loan middlemen

for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through committee (ordered reported 30–17 on July 21), and managed it to House passage 253–171 on September 17

for.name: 247 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage; only 4 Democrats voted no

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress to end the bank-based student loan program and redirect the savings to student aid, making the bill a White House priority

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 22, 2009 and never reported it out or held a vote; it sat until the Congress ended

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill after it was referred to his committee

against.name: 167 of 178 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage on September 17, 2009

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.what_they_did: Fought legislation ending the bank-based federal student loan program, on which their business model depended

sides.party_line_note: Passage split by party — 247 of 253 Democrats for, only 6 of 178 Republicans for — while the motion adding the Defund ACORN Act passed 345–75 with overwhelming bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders (FFEL program banks)
industries.note: The bill prohibits any new federally guaranteed loans under the bank-based FFEL program after June 30, 2010, ending the subsidy and guarantee payments private lenders receive for issuing student loans. Their federal loan business would have shifted entirely to direct federal lending.

industries.industry: Nonprofit student loan servicers and guaranty agencies
industries.note: Even as it eliminates bank lending, the bill locks these agencies into the new direct-lending system: the Education Secretary must contract with each state's nonprofit servicer for loans in that state at minimum business levels, pay job-retention incentives to servicers who hire former FFEL workers, and lets guaranty agencies compete for counseling, default-aversion, and grant subgrant roles. Their revenue channel survives the reform as a guaranteed part of the federal loan system.

The passed bill gives for-profit colleges three consecutive years (up from two) of failing the 90/10 rule requiring 10% of revenue from non-federal-aid sources before losing federal aid eligibility, and keeps counting certain 2008 loan-limit revenue as non-federal. This delays consequences for schools heavily dependent on federal student aid dollars.

industries.industry: Community colleges, historically Black colleges, and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: The bill funds community college facility construction and the American Graduation Initiative reform grants, extends HBCU and minority-serving institution funding through FY2019, and reserves a third of innovation-fund activity for two-year colleges. These institutions gain both money and students as aid expands.

Federal grants for public school and community college construction require payment of prevailing wages to laborers and mechanics and use of American-made iron and steel, directing public money toward union-scale construction work.
